newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai stocks set for more short-term gloom.
newsitem.headline: Thai stocks set for more short-term gloom.

text.p: Weaker economic growth prospects and fears over financing for the depressed Thai property sector are set to force the Thai stock index down to test 650 in the short term, analysts said on Monday.
The index ended last Friday at 702.10.
Upward pressure on Thai interest rates may grow if U.S. rates rise on Tuesday, further affecting Thai stocks and growth in an increasingly sluggish economy, they told Reuters.
The index has fallen over 40 percent in the past year and tumbled to near six-year lows this year on selling pressure, especially after this month's Thai finance sector crisis.

"Everybody is looking at GDP growth. I don't believe over six percent is possible any more...I would not disagree with a figure of around five percent," said Philip Adkins, head of research at Nava SC Securities.
Growth prospects have already been hit by a 106 billion baht (US$40 billion) government budget cut and slowing growth in the manufacturing sector, analysts said.
A possible Moody's downgrade of Thailand's long-term sovereign debt status and concerns surrounding the troubled property sector ensured the near-term outlook would be negative, analysts said.

"There is very little positive news...for the downside we might look at 650 first, and then if it goes through that, we could see the early 600 level," said Vason Thangkavivit, head of research at Pacific Finance and Securities.
Of immediate concern is the finance sector's loan exposure to troubled Thai property developers and the value of collateral pledged against those loans.

Doubts surrounding the viability of a 100 billion baht government scheme to issue zero coupon bonds to raise funds to relieve the finance sector of some bad loans to the real estate sector continued to weigh on sentiment, analysts said.
"The problems stem from the lack of disclosure and when you don't have enough to work with, it tends to be that you assume the worst," said a local fund manager.

Results of valuation on properties owned by developer Somprasong Plc, which failed to meet a $3.1 million Eurobond interest payment in February, are eagerly awaited for an accurate reflection of Bangkok property prices, analysts said.
"There is an expectation that property prices are 20, 30 or even 40 percent below their current book values but nobody knows for sure," said Adkins.

A drastic reduction in prices would force finance firms and banks to reassess the quality of the collateral backing loans and could further set back gloomy growth prospects in the financial sector this year, brokers said.

"They would probably just get away with a 25 percent reduction because banks usually lend up to 70 percent of appraised value so they would still be fully covered, ... but if it's 40 percent it would impact quite heavily," Adkins said.

Positive sentiment from a growing consensus that the baht would weather any future storms and the launch of new provident funds to liquidify the market were outweighed by loan concerns, analysts said.
"Our short-term outlook is negative but we are positive in the medium to long term...there is no rush to reinvest in Thailand and we have to see this problem with property sorted out," Adkins said.
